summary: The Transtubular potassium gradient calculator turns the serum potassium, the urine potassium and more into transtubular potassium gradient. It suits an informed starting point to take to a clinician, not a diagnosis. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Transtubular potassium gradient calculator work?
sections.html:
The Transtubular potassium gradient calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports transtubular potassium gradient in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the serum potassium, the urine potassium, the serum osmolality and the urine osmolality.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

sections.title: The formula behind the Transtubular potassium gradient calculator
sections.html:
One relationship drives the whole page:

Transtubular potassium gradient=(serum osmolality × urine potassium ÷ (serum potassium × urine osmolality))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Serum potassium = 10, Urine potassium = 10, Serum osmolality = 10 and Urine osmolality = 10. The calculator returns Transtubular potassium gradient = 1.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Transtubular potassium gradient = 1 should be roughly the size you expected from Serum potassium = 10 and Urine potassium = 10.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• A number, filled in as soon as the inputs allow it.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Transtubular potassium gradient calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Deciding whether a reading is worth a second look
  • Tracking a measurement over time and understanding what changed
  • Preparing for an appointment so you can describe your numbers clearly
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the serum potassium, the urine potassium and the serum osmolality — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.

sections.title: What are the limits worth knowing?
sections.html:
Every tool draws a boundary somewhere. For the Transtubular potassium gradient calculator, these are the ones that matter:

  • The calculator reports what the relationship implies; it does not judge whether the inputs themselves are sensible, so a figure that is out by a factor of ten will produce an answer that is out by the same factor.

sections.title: How do you check the answer yourself?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time — serum potassium for instance — and watch which results move. A result that stays put does not depend on it.
  • Try a round value you can work out in your head. If the answer matches your mental arithmetic, the inputs are on the scale you assumed.
  • Re-enter the same figure and confirm the result is stable; a number that moves when you press Calculate again is a sign that a field is still empty.

faq.q: What does the Transtubular potassium gradient calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns transtubular potassium gradient, derived from the serum potassium, the urine potassium and the serum osmolality. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Transtubular potassium gradient calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the serum potassium, the urine potassium, the serum osmolality and the urine osmolality, which is 4 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Transtubular potassium gradient = 1. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Transtubular potassium gradient calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. The calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.
